title: Timing Nerve Impulses and Muscle Spikes
endLine: Timing impulses gives nerve speed; muscle spikes track active motor units.

scenes.tts: How fast does a nerve signal race through a limb? And how can you read active muscle fibres under the skin? Two linked methods answer both. Nerve conduction velocity times axon impulses, while electromyography, or E M G, records muscle spikes.
scenes.caption: How fast does a nerve signal race through a limb? And how can you read active muscle fibres under the skin? Two linked methods answer both. Nerve conduction velocity times axon impulses, while electromyography, or EMG, records muscle spikes.
scenes.visual: Schematic side-view of a leg and lower spinal cord filling over 60% of frame height. A bright electrical impulse races along a peripheral nerve while skeletal muscle below twitches; question marks pulse over the hidden nerve and muscle. As the two methods are named, two markers highlight the nerve path and a live trace strip appears below the muscle (schematic).
scenes.narration: How fast does a nerve signal race through a limb? And how can you read active muscle fibres under the skin? Two linked methods answer both. Nerve conduction velocity times axon impulses, while electromyography, or EMG, records muscle spikes.

scenes.visual: The schematic leg softens slightly as the title 'Timing Nerve Impulses and Muscle Spikes' holds for 2.0 seconds over the gently pulsing nerve.

scenes.tts: An action potential is a brief, self-renewing electrical impulse. Response time adds each axon's length divided by its speed, plus delays at the ends. From one point, those end delays blur speed. Stimulate at two points, subtract arrival times, and shared end delays cancel.
scenes.caption: An action potential is a brief, self-renewing electrical impulse. Response time adds each axon's length divided by its speed, plus delays at the ends. From one point, those end delays blur speed. Stimulate at two points, subtract arrival times, and shared end delays cancel.
scenes.visual: On the carried schematic leg, focus on the motor nerve and muscle with a timing bar below. The formula 'time ≈ L/v + end delays' builds as spoken, with receptor, nerve-muscle junction, and muscle delay segments highlighted. A stimulus triggers at a near point (Point 1), then at a far point (Point 2); on the timing bar, the identical end-delay segments align and fade away, leaving only the travel time between the two points (schematic).
scenes.narration: An action potential is a brief, self-renewing electrical impulse. Response time adds each axon's length divided by its speed, plus delays at the ends. From one point, those end delays blur speed. Stimulate at two points, subtract arrival times, and shared end delays cancel.

scenes.tts: Dividing distance between those points by time difference gives conduction velocity, the impulse's speed. Speed rises with axon thickness and myelin, tight layers of glial membrane. Short bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, pack sodium channels densely. The impulse is renewed at each node, so it seems to jump: saltatory conduction.
scenes.caption: Dividing distance between those points by time difference gives conduction velocity, the impulse's speed. Speed rises with axon thickness and myelin, tight layers of glial membrane. Short bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, pack sodium channels densely. The impulse is renewed at each node, so it seems to jump: saltatory conduction.
scenes.visual: The equation 'v = distance / time' completes above the nerve, then the view zooms into the carried nerve shaft to show two neighbouring axons side by side: a thin bare axon and a thick axon wrapped in myelin sheaths from Schwann cells with short bare gaps labelled 'Nodes of Ranvier'. An electrical pulse creeps steadily along the bare axon while another leaps rapidly from node to node along the wrapped axon (schematic).
scenes.narration: Dividing distance between those points by time difference gives conduction velocity, the impulse's speed. Speed rises with axon thickness and myelin, tight layers of glial membrane. Short bare gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, pack sodium channels densely. The impulse is renewed at each node, so it seems to jump: saltatory conduction.

scenes.tts: Test the math on a one-metre path from foot to spinal cord, counting conduction alone. Travel time equals distance divided by speed. An unmyelinated C fibre can conduct at zero point five metres per second. How long does its impulse take to reach the cord?
scenes.caption: Test the math on a 1.00 m path from foot to spinal cord, counting conduction alone. Travel time equals distance divided by speed. An unmyelinated C fibre can conduct at 0.5 m/s. How long does its impulse take to reach the cord?
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full schematic leg marked with a '1.00 m' bracket from foot to spinal cord and the equation 't = L / v' at top right. A bare C fibre marker labelled '0.5 m/s' glows at the foot beside a large myelinated axon marker labelled '100 m/s'. A question card appears beside the cord: 'How long at 0.5 m/s over 1.00 m?' (leg anatomy schematic).
scenes.narration: Test the math on a 1.00 m path from foot to spinal cord, counting conduction alone. Travel time equals distance divided by speed. An unmyelinated C fibre can conduct at 0.5 m/s. How long does its impulse take to reach the cord?

scenes.visual: Hold the 1.00 m schematic leg, the formula 't = L / v', and the question card on screen for 4.5 seconds while a calm timer bar advances and the starting pulse glows gently at the foot.

scenes.tts: One metre divided by zero point five metres per second gives two seconds. At two metres per second, a C fibre takes zero point five seconds. Thinly myelinated A delta fibres run roughly five to thirty metres per second. Large myelinated axons at about a hundred metres per second take one hundredth of a second.
scenes.caption: 1.00 m divided by 0.5 m/s gives 2 seconds. At 2 m/s, a C fibre takes 0.5 seconds. Thinly myelinated Aδ fibres run roughly 5 to 30 m/s. Large myelinated axons at about 100 m/s take one hundredth of a second.
scenes.visual: Computed conduction race along the 1.00 m schematic leg (arrival times computed from t = L / v; anatomy schematic). Numbers substitute into 't = L / v' as spoken: the 0.5 m/s C fibre reaches the cord in 2 s; a 2 m/s C fibre arrives in 0.5 s; an Aδ fibre (5 to 30 m/s) pulls far ahead; and a large myelinated axon (about 100 m/s) flashes to the cord in one hundredth of a second.
scenes.narration: 1.00 m divided by 0.5 m/s gives 2 seconds. At 2 m/s, a C fibre takes 0.5 seconds. Thinly myelinated Aδ fibres run roughly 5 to 30 m/s. Large myelinated axons at about 100 m/s take one hundredth of a second.

scenes.tts: Now follow a motor axon to skeletal muscle. At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine starts an action potential along each fibre. One alpha motor neuron and its fibres form a motor unit. Fibres are not electrically connected, so each fires only when its own motor neuron fires. E M G records those muscle spikes, revealing active motor units.
scenes.caption: Now follow a motor axon to skeletal muscle. At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine starts an action potential along each fibre. scenes.visual: Follow the carried schematic pathway down an alpha motor neuron axon from the spinal cord to skeletal muscle. At the neuromuscular junction, a schematic release of acetylcholine triggers electrical pulses spreading along muscle fibre membranes and down T tubules. Two separate colour-coded motor units (fibres visibly unconnected) fire while an EMG trace strip below plots each unit's distinct spike train (schematic).
scenes.narration: Now follow a motor axon to skeletal muscle. At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine starts an action potential along each fibre. One alpha motor neuron and its fibres form a motor unit. Fibres are not electrically connected, so each fires only when its own motor neuron fires. EMG records those muscle spikes, revealing active motor units.

scenes.tts: Three guardrails keep records honest. Impulses are all-or-none, so stronger force adds firing rate and motor units, not taller spikes. A teaching model assumes about one millisecond per cord synapse, yet real synapses vary, so delay cannot prove the count. And some C fibres carry touch, not pain, so speed alone cannot fix what a fibre reports.
scenes.caption: Three guardrails keep records honest. Impulses are all-or-none, so stronger force adds firing rate and motor units, not taller spikes. A teaching model assumes about 1 ms per cord synapse, yet real synapses vary, so delay cannot prove the count. And some C fibres carry touch, not pain, so speed alone cannot fix what a fibre reports.
scenes.visual: Three transformations inside the carried schematic world: (1) On the EMG trace, spike height remains fixed while firing rate rises and a second motor unit joins as muscle pull grows; (2) A knee-jerk reflex loop through one cord synapse shows '~1 ms (varies)' with a badge 'Suggests, never proves'; (3) A slow C fibre branches to both touch and pain icons with a badge 'Speed alone ≠ report' (schematic).
scenes.narration: Three guardrails keep records honest. Impulses are all-or-none, so stronger force adds firing rate and motor units, not taller spikes. scenes.tts: In eighteen fifty, Helmholtz timed a frog nerve at two points: a few tens of metres per second. Later timing showed that thin bare fibres manage about one metre per second or less. The largest myelinated mammalian fibres reach about one hundred, or a little more.
scenes.caption: In 1850, Helmholtz timed a frog nerve at two points: a few tens of metres per second. Later timing showed that thin bare fibres manage about 1 metre per second or less. The largest myelinated mammalian fibres reach about 100, or a little more.
scenes.visual: Two milestone callouts build alongside the carried schematic nerve: first, Helmholtz (1850) two-point frog nerve timing ('few tens of m/s'); second, bare versus myelinated speed scale jumping from 'about 1 m/s or less' (thin bare fibres) to 'about 100 m/s or a bit more' (largest myelinated mammalian axons) (schematic).
scenes.narration: In 1850, Helmholtz timed a frog nerve at two points: a few tens of metres per second. Later timing showed that thin bare fibres manage about 1 metre per second or less. The largest myelinated mammalian fibres reach about 100, or a little more.

scenes.tts: On an E M G trace, graded force shows as more motor units firing, and firing more often. Time impulses across distance, and listen to muscle spikes, to test nerves and motor units together.
scenes.caption: On an EMG trace, graded force shows as more motor units firing, and firing more often. Time impulses across distance, and listen to muscle spikes, to test nerves and motor units together.
scenes.visual: Beside the muscle, the EMG strip shows pull grading up as more colour-coded motor units join and each fires more often (schematic, no data), then the full schematic limb pathway pulses in unison from nerve timing markers to muscle spikes.
scenes.narration: On an EMG trace, graded force shows as more motor units firing, and firing more often. Time impulses across distance, and listen to muscle spikes, to test nerves and motor units together.
